hooks.text: A dead star struck Earth from 20,000 light-years away.
A blast 20,000 light-years away physically punched our atmosphere.
Can a starquake 20,000 light-years away alter Earth's atmosphere?
20,000 light-years away, a dead star hit Earth.

title: The Starquake That Hit Earth
description: In 1998, a violent starquake on magnetar SGR 1900+14 unleashed a radiation blast so fierce it struck Earth from 20,000 light-years away.

beats.text: A dead star struck Earth from 20,000 light-years away.
beats.visual: Artist illustration of a magnetar surrounded by intense magnetic fields

beats.text: Spacecraft detectors across our solar system were suddenly blinded in August 1998.
beats.visual: Illustration of scientific satellite instruments overwhelmed by incoming radiation in orbit

beats.text: NASA's Rossi satellite was flooded by an invisible, pulsating gamma-ray wave.
beats.visual: Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer spacecraft operating in Earth orbit

beats.text: The signal flashed every 5.16 seconds from a magnetar called SGR 1900+14.
beats.visual: Diagram illustrating the spinning pulse profile of a neutron star

beats.text: Its magnetic field is trillions of times stronger than Earth's entire field.
beats.visual: Render of twisted magnetic field lines erupting from a neutron star crust

beats.text: Spitzer captured a seven light-year ring of glowing dust left behind.
beats.visual: Spitzer Space Telescope infrared image of the dust ring around SGR 1900+14, 2005

beats.text: The blast was powerful enough to physically alter Earth's atmosphere.
beats.visual: Artist illustration of gamma rays striking Earth's upper atmosphere

better_than_last: Applied reviewer revisions to beats 6 and 7, ensuring beat 7 directly loops into the hook while preserving the mystery structure.
